rv.q: As it has turned out, the show is still undermined by the remnants of a campy sensibility it could never fully replace with the dramatic poetry required by the stirring, feminist, nationalist story it so badly wanted to tell with passion and truth.
It just feels a little sad, as if a lot of people put a lot of time into something that's simply lifeless.
For all its inflamed passions, it never ignites.
Yet everything ultimately blurs into what feels like the aimless milling of a crowd on a carnival midway.
So over the top, it’s enough to make a feminist even angrier!
But in the end, a chorus line of flexible, well-oiled ankles can't elevate "The Pirate Queen" from being an ornate but empty treasure chest.
No blame can be pinned on the performers.

cn.t: Critics find this epic from the "Les Mis" creators loud, bombastic, and exhaustingly busy, with muddled storytelling that fails to deliver thrills despite its big scale and physical spectacle.

vs.sum: One of Broadway's largest houses (1,930 seats across four levels), the Lyric's sheer scale means rear orchestra and mezzanine seats sit far from the stage, with sightline obstructions from balcony overhangs. Acoustics are solid and the theater's modern construction makes it well-suited for spectacle productions.

acc.note: 42nd St entrance at street level with elevator to Orchestra and Dress Circle. No elevator to Balcony.
